When crustal shortening and mountain building occurs, the mountains encroach upon the basins, which leads to progressively larger grain sizes reflecting increasingly proximal deposition. We have observed these coarsening-upward sedimentary sequences all around the margin of the Tarim Basin, on both sides of the Tian Shan and within the Qaidam Basin; however, they are not necessarily coeval, even within a few millions of years. This is why we think that age con- straints solely based on facies correlation can have sig- nificant (10 – 20 Myr) errors. Pre-Cenozoic sediments are generally distinct from Cenozoic sediments and are fairly repetitive throughout central Asia. Cretaceous sediments are generally red to brick red, whereas Upper Jurassic red beds are interbedded with green sandstones and siltstones. Here again considerable overlap likely exists in time, which most probably leads to age uncertainties larger than those for the Cenozoic. Exceptions are in the western part of the Tarim Basin (and also in the Lhasa block) where fossiliferous Cretaceous and Paleogene marine carbonates crop out within the red bed sequences. Mesozoic to Recent Geology and Paleomagnetic Sampling [5] Sedimentary successions often crop out in the thrust packages exposed at the base of the mountains in central Asia. These, mainly Cenozoic, prograding sedimentary profiles are fairly monotonous throughout the region. The basal parts of the sequences are mainly fine-grained and represent deposition centers lying at some distance from the uplifting mountains. When crustal shortening and mountain building occurs, the mountains encroach upon the basins, which leads to progressively larger grain sizes reflecting increasingly proximal deposition. We have observed these coarsening-upward sedimentary sequences all around the margin of the Tarim Basin, on both sides of the Tian Shan and within the Qaidam Basin; however, they are not necessarily coeval, even within a few millions of years. Paleomagnetic constraints on the amount of displacement along the Altyn Tagh fault are difficult to establish because the fault’s easterly strike would require thousands of kilometers of offset in order to be resolvable by paleolatitude differences. One way around this problem is to use paleomagnetic rotations. First, if the Qaidam Basin rotated relative to the Tarim Basin, the relative motion must be mostly taken up by slip along the Altyn Tagh fault. Second, one can sample time- progressive sequences to determine when (or if) a partic- ular block had (or had not) rotated. A paleomagnetic study along the Altyn Tagh fault by Rumelhar

zes reflecting increasingly proximal deposition. We have observed these coarsening-upward sedimentary sequences all around the margin of the Tarim Basin, on both sides of the Tian Shan and within the Qaidam Basin; however, they are not necessarily coeval, even within a few millions of years. This is why we think that age con- straints solely based on facies correlation can have sig- nificant (10 – 20 Myr) errors. Pre-Cenozoic sediments are generally distinct from Cenozoic sediments and are fairly repetitive throughout central Asia. Cretaceous sediments are generally red to brick red, whereas Upper Jurassic red beds are interbedded with green sandstones and siltstones. Here again considerable overlap likely exists in time, which most probably leads to age uncertainties larger than those for the Cenozoic. Exceptions are in the western part of the Tarim Basin (and also in the Lhasa block) where fossiliferous Cretaceous and Paleogene marine carbonates crop out within the red bed sequences. Since 2002, the apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the YTT has been well deﬁned back to the mid-Early Cretaceous by several palaeopoles that show the YTT to be pericratonic since then (Symons et al. 2005, 2017). In this palaeomagnetic study we interpret the Ragged and Tatlmain intrusions to carry an Early Juras- sic overprint remanence. When the two overprint palaeopoles are added to the three previously published latest Triassic to Early Juras- sic palaeopoles, they show the YTT to have been accreted to the North American plate by the mid-Early Jurassic, which provides a constraint on tectonic models for the post-Triassic evolution of the YTT. 2G E O L O G Y Ragged stock and Tatlmain batholith intrude the YTT in the Glen- lyon map area (NTS 105 L/1–7, 11–14; 115I/9, 16) of central Yukon (Fig. 1). The resulting 196 ± 6 Ma Tatlmain and Ragged palaeopoles are 64.9 ◦N, 44.8◦E (A95 = 5.9◦) and 64.2 ◦N, 58.5◦E( A95 = 7.7◦), respectively. The YTT palaeopoles support para-autochthonous tectonic models that have the YTT: (1) accreting to North America by the Early Jurassic, (2) undergoing non-signiﬁcant orogen-perpendicular shortening by mid- Early Cretaceous from thrust-faulting, and, then (3) undergoing signiﬁcant orogen-parallel northward translation of ∼500 km from mid-Early Cretaceous to the Eocene. We speculate that ∼500 km of the northward translation is related to dextral motion on the Tintina and Northern Rocky Mountain Trench fault in British Columbia, and that the clockwise rotation is related to upper crustal tectonics in both Yukon and southern British Columbia. Con- versely, geologic evidence and palaeomagnetic work on several Cretaceous plutons have indicated that the YTT is pericratonic, having travelled ∼500 km northwards relative to North Amer- ica, mostly as a result of Palaeocene–Eocene dextral transcurrent fault displacement on the inboard Tintina fault zone (Gabrielse 1985; Symons et al. 2005; 2015, 2017; Gabrielse et al. 2006;M c - Causland et al. 2006; Symons & Kawasaki 2011). Received 2019 June 26; in original form 2018 November 27 SUMMARY The extensive Yukon-Tanana terrane (YTT) of the northern Canadian Cordillera has been considered controversially to be part of the allochthonous ‘Baja BC’ microcontinent or of the para-autochthonous North American cratonic margin during the Mesozoic. Palaeomagnetic methods have isolated a very-stable Early Jurassic thermochemical remanent remagnetization in the terrane’s felsic Tatlmain batholith and maﬁc Ragged stock after correction for: (1) rotation from northeast-plunging anticlinal deformation, (2) northerly dipping tectonic tilt of the host rocks and (3) northwestward regional translation on the adjacent Tintina transcurrent fault zone. The resulting 196 ± 6 Ma Tatlmain and Ragged palaeopoles are 64.9 ◦N, 44.8◦E (A95 = 5.9◦) and 64.2 ◦N, 58.5◦E( A95 = 7.7◦), respectively. The YTT palaeopoles support para-autochthonous tectonic models that have the YTT: (1) accreting to North America by the Early Jurassic, (2) undergoing non-signiﬁcant orogen-perpendicular shortening by mid- Early Cretaceous from thrust-faulting, and, then (3) undergoing signiﬁcant orogen-parallel northward translation of ∼500 km from mid-Early Cretaceous to the E

We speculate that ∼500 km of the northward translation is related to dextral motion on the Tintina and Northern Rocky Mountain Trench fault in British Columbia, and that the clockwise rotation is related to upper crustal tectonics in both Yukon and southern British Columbia. Introduction Large igneous provinces (LIPs) are magmatic provinces that cover areas greater than 100,000 km 2, contain igneous volumes exceeding 100,000 km 3, and are usually characterized by an intense eruptive pulse(s) of short duration ( –5 Myr)

al rela- tionship with the KMP. Considering that (1) some published latest Jurassic and Early Cretaceous paleomagnetic data from the TH lack robust ﬁeld tests to question the reliability of the data ( Klootwijk and Bingham, 1980; Zhu et al., 1981; Patzelt et al., 1996; Li et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2015 ); and (2) although these Jurassic and Cre- taceous igneous rocks have an overall similarity in geochemical characteristics to the KMP (e.g., Zhu et al., 2007, 2008; Shi et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2022 ), the spatial relationship of these latest Jurassic and Early Cretaceous igneous rocks to the KMP is an essential prerequisite for understanding the causal link between the eastern Gondwana breakup and the KMP, additional reliable latest Jurassic and Early Cretaceous paleomagnetic data- sets with well-established ages constraint from the TH are still required to address the aforementioned issues. In this study, we present an analysis of paleomagnetic data on the Zhela Formation (Fm.) basalts and sandstones in the Taga area of the eastern TH. The new results allow us to constrain the pale- ogeography of the TH during the latest Jurassic to Early Cretaceous and thus provide a better understanding of the causal link between the CBLIP and the KMP. 2. Most VGPs remain in the northern hemisphere (positive latitudes) at high latitudes ( > 60 ◦ ), with a few migrating to the southern hemisphere but only reaching medium lati - tudes, compatible with an excursion and not a complete reversal of the geomagnetic field. However, at the base of sections 1 to 3 , the variability of the VGPs suggests a recovering field from a reversal. The topmost sections, 6 and 7, exhibit different behavior than the others, with their VGPs at medium latitudes in the base and a complete reversal on the top of the sequences between elevations 772 – 774 m. The reversed magne - tization component is of primary origin and remains stable during de - magnetizations up to 80 mT or 600 ◦ C. This reversed field was probably imparted as a soft secondary component in a few samples of sections 1 and 2 , as mentioned before and seen in Figs. 3 and 5 . On the stereogram of Fig. 8 , the distribution of the VGPs calculated after the inclination correction shows a tight cluster near the geographic pole corresponding mainly to the results from sections 1 to 5 and a higher dispersion of data from sections 6 and 7. Most of these VGPs plot outside the polar cap delimited by the parallel 45 ◦ , compatible with a varying field as was the field at the end of the Cretaceous Normal Superchron (CNS), which lasted from ~126 to 84 Ma ( He et al., 2012 ). Notably, the Uberaba Formation, which occupies a restricted area in the northeastern portion of the basin ( Fig. 1 ), is in contact with the Serra Geral basalts. Despite this, its depositional characteristics indicate contributions from the Late Cretaceous Alto Paranaiba alkaline volcanism to the north ( Ferreira Júnior and Gomes, 1999 ). Previous magnetostratigraphic research on the Uberaba Formation placed it in the Campanian-Maastrichtian ( Tamrat et al., 2002 ), and the authors identified some polarity intervals loosely correlated with the geomagnetic polarity time scale. However, the rough data was never fully published, and no paleomagnetic pole was calculated. n the Bauru Group, was deposited over the Early Cretaceous volcanic rocks of the Paran ´a Basin in southern Brazil. It occupies a restricted northeastern area of the basin surrounding the homonymous city. Recent works on stratigraphy and paleontology indicate a Campanian age, a novel finding that challenges the previously held belief of a Cenomanian age based on dinosaur bones. Paleomagnetic work on seven sections of the Uberaba formation has resulted in the calculation of a paleo - magnetic pole at 82.2 ◦ S 350.8 ◦ E (N = 89; k = 23; A 95 = 3.2 ◦ ) after correcting for the shallowing of the magnetic inclination caused by overload. The formation is dated to ~73 Ma (Campanian) age based on magnetostrati - graphic data and comparisons with other Late Cretaceous poles. The area stayed as a highland until the tectonic events related to the northward emplacement of the alkaline provinces. Isothermal remanent magnetization IRM curves ( Fig. 3 ) show a fast increase of remanence acquisition at low fields, but saturation is not reached at fields lower than 2000 mT ( Table 1 ). The backfield curves ( Fig. 3 ) show remanence coercivity between 300 and 500 mT ( Table 1 ). These procedures suggest the presence of both hematite and magnetite phases. Fig. 3 and Table 2 show the results of the analysis of separation of magnetic components. Three components were identified in both sam - ples: i) one with coercivity values of 76 and 96 mT that may correspond to magnetite, ii) an intermediate coercivity (377 – 393 mT) that corre - sponds to hematite, and iii) a high coercivity component (3421 and 3454 mT) that was not completely saturated and may correspond to goethite. Magnetite component show high dispersion values, which is typical of sedimentary and/or detritical origin ( Egli, 2004 ). The relative proportion between the components indicate the larger presence of hematite in the samples. Methods All demagnetization treatments and remanence measurements were performed in a shielded room with residual fields less than 300 nT at South China Sea Institute of Oceanology. Most of the samples were treated with stepwise thermal demagnetiza- tion. Some samples were also progressively demagnetized using alternating fields. The remanence after each step was measured on a 2G cryogenic magnetometer. Rock magnetic experiments were performed at the University of California, Santa Cruz. Magnetic hysteresis curves were measured on a Princeton Measurements MicroMag 2900 alternating gradient. The temperature versus susceptibility curves were mea- sured using a Kappabridge KLY-2 susceptibility bridge with a CS-2 furnace. Palaeomagnetic directions were identified using principal component analysis to obtain a best-fitting demagnetization trajectory 56. A few samples were analyzed with great circle methods 57. (2022) suggested that the Lhasa terrane in the Late Cretaceous was located at ~ 11-15 ◦ N in a WNW-ESE orientation. Notably, its shape during the early Eocene remains poorly understood. Finally, most of the previous results were from the interior part of the Lhasa terrane; only paleomagnetic studies from the Xigaze forearc basin can truly represent the southern margin of Asia before the India – Asia collision and do not need to consider potential crustal shortening within the Lhasa terrane ( Meng et al., 2012; Li et al., 2022 ). More reliable paleomagnetic results from the Xigaze forearc basin would be useful for providing further constraints on the paleogeography of the southern margin of the Lhasa terrane during the late Paleocene. Therefore, we conducted paleomagnetic studies on the upper Paleocene (Thanetian stage) Jialazi Formation within the Xigaze forearc basin. 2. Geological setting and sampling The Tibetan Plateau presents a complex orogenic collage primarily composed of distinct tectonic units arranged from north to south, including the Songpan – Ganze terrane, Qiangtang terrane, Lhasa terrane, and Himalayas ( Yin and Harrison, 2000 ) ( Fig. 1 a). These units are delineated by prominent sut

thys, respectively ( Gehrels et al., 2011; Metcalfe, 2013 ). The Lhasa terrane is segmented into southern and northern subterranes ( Wang et al., 2022 ), with the Gangdese (or Transhimalayan) magmatic arc prevailing in the southern section, primarily consisting of Mesozoic to Eocene intrusive and extrusive igneous rocks ( Kapp and DeCelles, 2019 ). To the south of the Lhasa terrane, the IYS features Xigaze forearc basin (XFB) and the Xigaze accretionary complex, which include ophiolites and m ´elanges ( Kapp and DeCelles, 2019; Wang et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2013 ). The Xigaze ophiolite, often in tectonic contact with forearc sediments, is posited as the basement for the forearc strata ( Huang et al., 2015 ). Stretching more than 500 km from Renbu in the east to Zhongba in the west, the XFB extends along the Yarlung Zangbo River in an east – west orientation ( Wang et al., 2012 ). Isolated remnants of forearc sediments are sporadically found in the Zanda area ( Sun et al., 2018 ). The XFB, dating from the Early Cretaceous to the Eocene, is exposed as an east – west trending syncline with a westward inclination ( Metcalf and Kapp, 2019 ). (2022) suggested that the Lhasa terrane in the Late Cretaceous was located at ~ 11-15 ◦ N in a WNW-ESE orientation. Notably, its shape during the early Eocene remains poorly understood. Finally, most of the previous results were from the interior part of the Lhasa terrane; only paleomagnetic studies from the Xigaze forearc basin can truly represent the southern margin of Asia before the India – Asia collision and do not need to consider potential crustal shortening within the Lhasa terrane ( Meng et al., 2012; Li et al., 2022 ). More reliable paleomagnetic results from the Xigaze forearc basin would be useful for providing further constraints on the paleogeography of the southern margin of the Lhasa terrane during the late Paleocene. Therefore, we conducted paleomagnetic studies on the upper Paleocene (Thanetian stage) Jialazi Formation within the Xigaze forearc basin. 2. Geological setting and sampling The Tibetan Plateau presents a complex orogenic collage primarily composed of distinct tectonic units arranged from north to south, including the Songpan – Ganze terrane, Qiangtang terrane, Lhasa terrane, and Himalayas ( Yin and Harrison, 2000 ) ( Fig. 1 a). These units are delineated by prominent sut

thys, respectively ( Gehrels et al., 2011; Metcalfe, 2013 ). The Lhasa terrane is segmented into southern and northern subterranes ( Wang et al., 2022 ), with the Gangdese (or Transhimalayan) magmatic arc prevailing in the southern section, primarily consisting of Mesozoic to Eocene intrusive and extrusive igneous rocks ( Kapp and DeCelles, 2019 ). The Xigaze ophiolite, often in tectonic contact with forearc sediments, is posited as the basement for the forearc strata ( Huang et al., 2015 ). Conclusions Our magnetostratigraphic data allows the construction of the first geomagnetic polarity chronostratigraphic scale for the ca.10.4 Myr of the Llandovery, ranging into the earliest Wenlock. This is defined using polarity data from six sections, a dataset supported by fold and reversal tests, indicating the primary nature of the magnetisations, which is carried by variable mixtures of both haematite and magnetite. At the Backside Beck section, directional data is consistent with previous palaeomagnetic data from the area. We construct a correlation and age framework onto which these magnetostratigraphic datasets are linked, using: a) existing graptolite biostratigraphy b) correlations using carbon isotope changes, and c) magnetic susceptibility data for within UK sec - tion correlations . The polarity boundaries are generally rather loosely tied to the graptolite biozones for most of this interval, and will require more work to improve cross-calibration. Conclusions Our magnetostratigraphic data allows the construction of the first geomagnetic polarity chronostratigraphic scale for the ca.10.4 Myr of the Llandovery, ranging into the earliest Wenlock. This is defined using polarity data from six sections, a dataset supported by fold and reversal tests, indicating the primary nature of the magnetisations, which is carried by variable mixtures of both haematite and magnetite. At the Backside Beck section, directional data is consistent with previous palaeomagnetic data from the area. We construct a correlation and age framework onto which these magnetostratigraphic datasets are linked, using: a) existing graptolite biostratigraphy b) correlations using carbon isotope changes, and c) magnetic susceptibility data for within UK sec - tion correlations . The polarity boundaries are generally rather loosely tied to the graptolite biozones for most of this interval, and will require more work to improve cross-calibration. Conclusions Our magnetostratigraphic data allows the construction of the first geomagnetic polarity chronostratigraphic scale for the ca.10.4 Myr of the Llandovery, ranging into the earliest Wenlock. This is defined using polarity data from six sections, a dataset supported by fold and reversal tests, indicating the primary nature of the magnetisations, which is carried by variable mixtures of both haematite and magnetite. At the Backside Beck section, directional data is consistent with previous palaeomagnetic data from the area. We construct a correlation and age framework onto which these magnetostratigraphic datasets are linked, using: a) existing graptolite biostratigraphy b) correlations using carbon isotope changes, and c) magnetic susceptibility data for within UK sec - tion correlations . The polarity boundaries are generally rather loosely tied to the graptolite biozones for most of this interval, and will require more work to improve cross-calibration. Magnetic mineralogy The magnetic properties of samples from the sections and cores range from hard to soft coercivity behaviour, with high coercivity minerals (haematite, goethite) seen by the non-saturation at 300 mT IRM fields ( Fig. 9 a,e), and remanent coercivity (Hcr) > 200 mT (SI Fig. S8). At Backside Beck the red-samples from the Hebblethwaite Mbr, and some non-red samples from the Browgill Fm have > 80% of IRM acquisition above 200 mT and Hcr > 280 mT ( Fig. 9 a). Similar behaviour is seen to dominate the reddish lithologies from Hillend Farm and Buttington Quarry ( Fig. 9 e). Conclusions Our magnetostratigraphic data allows the construction of the first geomagnetic polarity chronostratigraphic scale for the ca.10.4 Myr of the Llandovery, ranging into the earliest Wenlock. This is defined using polarity data from six sections, a dataset supported by fold and reversal tests, indicating the primary nature of the magnetisations, which is carried by variable mixtures of both haematite and magnetite. At the Backside Beck section, directional data is consistent with previous palaeomagnetic data from the area. We construct a correlation and age framework onto which these magnetostratigraphic datasets are linked, using: a) existing graptolite biostratigraphy b) correlations using carbon isotope changes, and c) magnetic susceptibility data for within UK sec - tion correlations . The polarity boundaries are generally rather loosely tied to the graptolite biozones for most of this interval, and will require more work to improve cross-calibration. Magnetic results 4.1. Magnetic mineralogy The magnetic properties of samples from the sections and cores range from hard to soft coercivity behaviour, with high coercivity minerals (haematite, goethite) seen by the non-saturation at 300 mT IRM fields ( Fig. 9 a,e), and remanent coercivity (Hcr) > 200 mT (SI Fig. S8). At Backside Beck the red-samples from the Hebblethwaite Mbr, and some non-red samples from the Browgill Fm have > 80% of IRM acquisition above 200 mT and Hcr > 280 mT ( Fig. 9 a). Similar behaviour is seen to dominate the reddish lithologies from Hillend Farm and Buttington Quarry ( Fig. 9 e). The hard ferrimagnetic mineral in most of these sam - ples is haematite as shown by the resistance of the NRM to thermal demagnetisation (see later). Fig. 6. Detailed magnetic and organic matter car

the Silurian at Bardo Stawy (Zbra Fm), Grabowiec-6, Core-A and grey lithologies at Butting - ton Quarry have some of the softest behaviour (H cr < 35 mT; SI Fig. s8), but with some of these also having 10 – 20% IRM acquisition above 200 mT ( Fig. 9 b,d,e). Behaviours intermediate between these hard and soft end members are found at Backside Beck and Bardo Stawy (Rembow Fm; Fig. 9 a,b). The relative consistency of the Hcr and IRM 1T / χ ARM values in those samples with soft coercivity behaviour, suggest a similar miner - alogy in most of the sections and cores. Using the data in Peters and Dekkers (2003) suggests this is most likely magnetite, with magnetic particle sizes < 0.1 μ m in size (SI Fig. S8). 4.2. Magnetic fabric At Backside Beck the MS is largely carried by paramagnetic minerals ( English 1999 ; SI Fig. S9), and so the AMS represents paramagnetic mineral crystallographic alignments. Conclusions Our magnetostratigraphic data allows the construction of the first geomagnetic polarity chronostratigraphic scale for the ca.10.4 Myr of the Llandovery, ranging into the earliest Wenlock. This is defined using polarity data from six sections, a dataset supported by fold and reversal tests, indicating the primary nature of the magnetisations, which is carried by variable mixtures of both haematite and magnetite. At the Backside Beck section, directional data is consistent with previous palaeomagnetic data from the area. We construct a correlation and age framework onto which these magnetostratigraphic datasets are linked, using: a) existing graptolite biostratigraphy b) correlations using carbon isotope changes, and c) magnetic susceptibility data for within UK sec - tion correlations . The polarity boundaries are generally rather loosely tied to the graptolite biozones for most of this interval, and will require more work to improve cross-calibration. In summary, samples from twenty-two intervals display reversed polarity up to 580°C, and then dis- play Early Jurassic normal polarity at higher temperatures, typically at 645°C. Generally these samples display Jurassic normal polarity at only one demagnetization temperature, and return to reversed or intermediate directions in high tem- perature steps. Overall, the Kayenta Formation largely recorded re- versed polarity, but 9 to 11 short intervals present short nor- mal polarity intervals (Fig. 4). Among the demagnetized samples, 9 intervals display clear normal polarity and two additional intervals also may record normal polarity, but have larger uncertainties. These normal polarity intervals were obvious in NRM directions as well as demagnetized directions. Acquisition, preparation, measurement and demagnetization All samples were obtained as oriented cores in the field using stan - dard methods. In the Pacific Northwest Paleomagnetism Laboratory at the Western Washington University, the 2.5 cm in diameters cores were sliced into specimens 2.2 cm in length. Remanent magnetization was measured with a 2G Enterprise model 755 three-axis DC-SQUID magnetometer in a magnetically shielded room, which has an internal field of less than 350 nT. We conducted a detailed rock magnetic and magnetostratigraphic study of the Cretaceous Jiaguan and Guankou Formations (the Jinmenguan section) within the Longmenshan foreland basin on the eastern edge of Tibetan Plateau. Inclination Shallowing Correction Paleomagnetic directions of hematite‐bearing and fine‐grained detrital sedimentary rocks may have suffered from depositional and /or compaction‐induced inclination shallowing (Kodama, 2012 ; Tauxe & Kent, 2004 ). The relationship between the inclination observed from specimens ( I o ) and the applied magnetic field inclination ( I f ) can be described as the formula: tan ( I o ) = f tan ( I f ), where f is the flattening factor (King, 1955 ). In this study, the HTC directions display an east‐west elongated distribution (Figure 8b ), which is an important indicator of inclination shallowing (Tauxe & Kent, 2004 ). Magmatic activity is concentrated along the WFB and the rift marginal Silti-Debre Zeit Fault Zone (SDFZ) belt, with mafic volcanism occurring along these zones in the form of numerous mono - genetic basaltic vents, such as spatter cones, scoria cones, and maars ( Rooney et al., 2007 , 2014a ; Maccaferri et al., 2014 ; Mazzarini et al., 2013 ). The central MER ( Fig. 1 ) exhibits reduced tectonomagmatic ac - tivity proceeding southward from the northern MER sector ( Keranen and Klemperer, 2008 ). Core samples were taken from ignimbrite (~1.7 – 2.54Ma), basalt, and trachyte rock units ( < 1.6Ma) along the western margin of the central MER. Each core sample underwent analysis using twin specimens subjected to stepwise alternate field (AF) and thermal (Th) demagnetization techniques. Furthermore, a single specimen from every site was employed for rock-magnetic experiments. Detailed rock magnetic experiments identified titano-magnetite, magnetite, and hematite as the remanence carrier magnetic minerals. The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) directional analysis revealed two components:1) a low-stability (LS) component removed by low- temperature ( < 300 ◦ C) and low-field ( < 20 mT) and 2) a high-stability (HS) with heating > 300 ◦ C or 20 mT increments showed vectors pointing to the plot ’ s origin, indicative of the characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM). All sites, except one, displayed reverse polarity NRM. Hypotheses to explain these data include rapid true polar wander (TPW), a geomagnetic field geometry that deviates from a predominantly axial dipole field, a hyper‐reversing field ( > 10 reversals/Ma), and/or undiagnosed remagnetization. To test these hypotheses, we collected 1,057 oriented cores over a 85 m stratigraphic succession in the Laoshanya Formation (Yangjiaping, Hunan, China). High precision U‐Pb dating of two intercalated tuff layers constrain the age of the sediments between 809 and 804 Ma. Thermal demagnetization isolates three magnetization components residing in hematite which are not time‐progressive but conflated throughout the section. All samples possess a north and downward directed component in geographic coordinates at temperatures up to 660°C that is ascribed to a Cretaceous overprint. Two components isolated above 660°C reveal distinct directional clusters: one is interpreted as a depositional remanence, while the other appears to be the result of a mid‐Paleozoic (460 to 420 Ma) remagnetization, which is likely widespread throughout South China. The Yangjiaping (Hunan Province, China) area has a fairly complete geologic record from the Neoproterozoic through the Paleozoic, including Marinoan tillites and cap carbonates (Macouin et al., 2004 ). Below the tillites lie the Laoshanya Formation red beds, which were previously dated at Yangjiaping to 809 ± 16 Ma (Yin et al., 2003 ). There, we collected 1,057 paleomagnetic cores in a 85 metre‐thick section, freshly exposed along a river, as well as 14 cores in the underlying Lengjiaxi Group. We present a paleomagnetic study of those samples, combined with rock magnetic, mineralogical and microscopic analyses, as well as ID‐TIMS U‐Pb zircon geochronology of intercalated tuffs, in order to shed light on Neoproterozoic geomagnetic field behavior and the paleogeography of South China around 820 to 800 Ma.
